key_concept: A child with blood group O must be homozygous $ii$, so each parent must carry and pass on at least one recessive $i$ allele.
steps: Blood group O has only one genotype, $ii$. A child is O only if it receives one $i$ from the father and one $i$ from the mother.
Option (1): $I^A i \times I^B i$ gives $I^AI^B$, $I^A i$, $I^B i$ and $ii$, each with probability $\frac{1}{4}$. An O child is possible.
Option (2): $I^A i \times I^A i$ gives $I^AI^A : I^A i : ii = 1:2:1$. An O child is possible with probability $\frac{1}{4}$.
Option (3): $I^B i \times I^B i$ gives $I^BI^B : I^B i : ii = 1:2:1$. An O child is possible with probability $\frac{1}{4}$.

Option (4): the father $I^AI^B$ (blood group AB) has no $i$ allele. Every child receives either $I^A$ or $I^B$ from him, so the possible genotypes are $I^AI^A$, $I^A i$, $I^AI^B$ and $I^B i$. An $ii$ child is impossible.
So the combination in option (4) cannot produce a child with blood group O.
final_answer: Option (4): Father : $I^A I^B$ and Mother : $I^A i$
why_not_others: In options (1), (2) and (3), both parents are heterozygous with $i$, so each can pass on $i$ and an $ii$ (O) child has a $\frac{1}{4}$ chance. Only option (4) has a parent with no $i$ allele.
common_trap: Students think only about the parents' phenotypes (for example, 'A and B parents cannot have an O child') instead of checking whether each parent's genotype carries the $i$ allele.
time_saving_tip: Just check whether each parent carries $i$. Any parent with genotype $I^AI^B$, $I^AI^A$ or $I^BI^B$ rules out an O child immediately.
